title: Also the audience was going nuts, which made it even more fun! #broad...
transcript: Not only is Paranormal Activity on stage a rare horror play on Broadway, it's also a bit of a Dream Team collab between the creator of Sleep No More and the writer of Grey House. Director Felix Barrett and playwright Levi Holloway have created a new story under the branding of the Paranormal Activity franchise, drawing some narrative fragments from the film but otherwise telling a standalone story. As I've said in some recent videos, I'm always excited to see some genuinely frightening horror on stage. Where it feels like most horror theater kind of flirts with the genre, includes maybe a few jump scares, but otherwise doesn't fully commit to the thrills and chills popcorn horror experience, but I think this one really does. They even literally sell popcorn at the theater. It does take a little while to get going, and in the first part of the show there's maybe a few too many cheap fake outs, just relying heavily on ear piercingly loud sounds to scare the audience instead of the actual content. But I was pretty captivated from beginning to end. And ultimately I do think it delivers on the frights, both in terms of the jump scares and in general the eerie, uncanny phenomena as they're haunted by this entity. All of which were aided by the cool special effects, which were pretty classic, but no less impressive because of it. I won't spoil anything, but interestingly there is a major plot point that echoes Grey House a little bit, which kind of made it feel almost like a companion piece within Levi Holloway's body of work. He doesn't give us easy answers, but does make us feel like there's something worth latching onto narratively and thematically. So we leave the theater maybe a little confused, but also curious to unriddle it. I have to admit I'm still not totally sure what was going on, although it's clear that the central theme has to do with the baggage that each of these people carry with them and into their marriage. But I'm not positive whether the disparate pieces quite add up. I don't think the post show unriddling has been quite as rewarding for me as it was for Grey House, at least so far. So I kinda feel like this show is a little too good to just be pure schlocky horror fun, but not quite finely chiseled enough to stand on its own as a narrative play. But still. I was very entertained by it, and actually I watched the original film afterward, and to be honest, I think the play is more satisfying and maybe even more frightening.
reasoning: Reviewer clearly recommends the show, praising the scares, special effects, and being captivated throughout, while noting narrative shortcomings and cheap fake-outs early on. Ends favorably by saying the play is more satisfying than the film.
